title: Draupadi's question
hook: Vidura tells the hall of Prahlada, a father who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely

segments.voice: Yesterday Karna tried to make Draupadi's question unnecessary, arguing from the elders' silence, and the cloth kept coming. Did you notice silence being counted as agreement? Day seven hundred seventy-four.

The heap of cloth lies on the floor. The hall is shaken, and still no one has answered Draupadi. So Vidura stands, and instead of an argument, he tells an old story. It's about a judge asked to decide a case in which his own son was one of the two sides. The question for him was simple and terrible: will you tell the truth if it costs your own child? Today, Vidura's story of Prahlada.
screen: `STILL NO ONE HAS ANSWERED.` → `VIDURA TELLS A STORY.` → `A JUDGE, AND HIS OWN SON.`

segments.voice: Vidura begins by speaking to the hall. Draupadi has asked a question, he says, and it must be answered. Someone who knows the answer and stays silent shares in the wrong, he says, and so does someone who answers falsely. Then the story. Two young men, Virochana, Prahlada's son, and Sudhanvan, a Brahmin's son, quarreled over which of them was the greater, and they staked their lives on it. They went to Prahlada, Virochana's own father, to judge between them. Sudhanvan warned him: answer falsely, or not at all, and you'll suffer for it. Prahlada, troubled, went to the sage Kashyapa and asked what becomes of one who won't answer, or who answers wrongly. Kashyapa told him that such a person carries a heavy burden of wrong. So Prahlada came back and gave his verdict, against his own son. Sudhanvan is the greater, he said, and Sudhanvan's father is greater than I am. And Sudhanvan, moved by that honesty, gave Virochana's life back to his father. Then Vidura turns to the kings and elders and says, in effect: you've heard it. Now think, and answer her. Set that story down in this hall. Prahlada had every reason to tilt the truth: it was his own son. He didn't. The kings in the hall have far less at stake than he did, and still they won't speak. The telling says that even after Vidura's story, the kings said nothing at all.
screen: `VIDURA: SILENCE SHARES IN THE WRONG.` · `TWO YOUNG MEN, ONE QUARREL.` · `PRAHLADA JUDGES AGAINST HIS SON.` · `STILL THE KINGS SAY NOTHING.` · then, large: `ANSWER HER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind a question someone has asked you, or asked a group you're part of, that's still waiting for an honest answer. Maybe the honest answer costs something: a friendship, some pride, an advantage for your own side. Don't answer it now. Just let yourself see what the honest answer would be, quietly, the way Prahlada had to. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can bring that question into your prayer. If not, simply rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's question. Vidura tells of Prahlada, who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely, and asks the hall to answer her.
Your line: Draupadi's question. Today, when an honest answer would cost your own side something, see if you can give it anyway, kindly. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Vidura's story of Prahlada's honest verdict is retold as a lesson about speaking truly in a council.

myth: Prahlada ruled in favor of his own son
he judged that Sudhanvan was the greater, against his son Virochana.
Vidura said that keeping silent when you know the answer shares in the wrong
he said both silence and a false answer carry fault.
after Vidura's story, the kings answered Draupadi
the telling says they still said nothing.

fork.setup: you're Prahlada. your son and a Brahmin's son ask you to judge between them, and the truth is against your son. what do you do?
options: tell the truth, against your son.
fork.reveal: after asking the sage Kashyapa, he judges for Sudhanvan, and Sudhanvan gives Virochana's life back to his father.

original.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, what Prahlada chose over his own son's cause.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old fable dropped into the middle of a crisis.
what it means: a story about answering truly when it costs your own, told to a hall that won't answer.
what a scholar hears: the poem meets the hall's silence with a story inside a story, and the inner story judges the outer hall.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Vidura's address to the assembly; the story of Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan, and Prahlada's question to Kashyapa; the kings' silence)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Vidura's teaching that one who knows and does not answer, and one who answers falsely, both incur sin (Ganguli gives proportions of the sin; left out).

Confirm the Prahlada story details: Virochana and Sudhanvan quarrel (over a maiden in some tellings; left out) and stake their lives; Prahlada consults Kashyapa; Prahlada says Sudhanvan and Angiras (Sudhanvan's father) are superior; Sudhanvan returns Virochana's life.
Confirm that the kings said nothing after Vidura spoke.
Placement: the script follows the order in which Ganguli has Vidura speak after the disrobing; confirm.
howItsDone calls Prahlada a great devotee of Vishnu, from the Puranic tradition, not this passage; confirm framing.
Editor: teach no longer tells the listener what to feel; howItsDone drops the 'great devotee of Vishnu' claim, which the cited passage does not make.
